answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: born 1964 · Founder of Amazon; founder of Blue Origin
answer.sourceLine: Widely and credibly credited to Bezos, and entirely consistent with Amazon’s deliberately thin-margin strategy — but no dated speech, interview, letter or filing has ever been produced. The earliest documented appearance is a November 2012 Fortune cover story that calls it “a favorite Bezos aphorism” in the journalist’s own voice, not a remark captured on the record.
answer.confidenceText: Credibly Bezos-shaped, but never sourced to a documented occasion.

Reported aphorism in the journalist’s voice — not a transcribed Bezos quotation, and no occasion is named

source.excerpt: A favorite Bezos aphorism is ‘Your margin is my opportunity.’ … Amazon sells at the bare minimum needed to break even, on the assumption it will make money elsewhere.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ investigated the line in January 2019 and reports that its earliest match appeared in November 2012 in Fortune. Its verdict is deliberately unfinished: the evidence that Bezos employed the quotation is substantive, but QI does not know whether Lashinsky or anyone else heard it directly from him.

Reading the Fortune article ↗ confirms the shape of the problem. The sentence is there, dated 16 November 2012 and flagged as being from the 3 December 2012 issue — but it arrives as “a favorite Bezos aphorism,” with no occasion, date or interview attached.
The reference chain doubles back. Wikiquote ↗ carries the line under plain “Quotes” on the strength of one citation, a 2019 Forbes column ↗ — which credits Bezos and links back to Quote Investigator.
Checking his own published writing turns up nothing. The phrase does not appear in Bezos’s 2020 letter to shareholders ↗, his last as chief executive, which reprints the 1997 letter in full.
source.excerptNote: Note whose sentence this is. Lashinsky is describing a habit of mind, not reporting a moment — there is no meeting, no date, no interlocutor. Every later version that supplies those details supplies them from somewhere other than this article.
source.rightsHolder: Adam Lashinsky and Fortune (2012 article). No rights holder is identifiable for the underlying remark, because no published source for it has been located.
source.rightsNote: The only documented text carrying this sentence is Adam Lashinsky’s Fortune cover story, first published 16 November 2012 and therefore firmly in copyright. If Bezos originated the remark in speech, no dated, published record of that utterance has been identified — so there is no earlier work whose rights could be assessed, and no basis whatever for treating the line as public domain.

author.name: Jeff Bezos
author.kicker: The man the line is pinned on
author.heading: About Jeff Bezos
author.metaLine: born 12 January 1964 · American businessman · founder of Amazon & Blue Origin
author.bio: Jeffrey Preston Bezos founded Amazon in 1994 and ran it as chief executive until 5 July 2021, when he became executive chairman; he also founded the spaceflight company Blue Origin in 2000. His signature strategic move was refusing to defend fat profit margins — pricing at close to break-even and betting that scale, selection and speed would pay later. That posture is exactly why this aphorism sticks to him so readily, and exactly why it is so rarely checked.

misattribution.heading: What gets overclaimed
misattribution.intro: Nobody credits this line to the wrong person — the problem is the opposite. It is credited to the right person with a confidence the record does not support, and the citation trail loops back on itself rather than reaching a source.

items.why: The line is reproduced in quotation marks with a speaker tag across business writing, but no dated speech, interview, letter or filing containing it has been produced. Quote Investigator ↗ calls the evidence substantive while stating it does not know whether Lashinsky or anyone else heard the statement directly from Bezos.

Wikiquote ↗ lists the line under plain “Quotes” with a single citation: Ron Shevlin’s 2019 Forbes piece. That column ↗ credits Bezos and hyperlinks Quote Investigator — so the apparent second source is the first source wearing a hat.

Later versions place the remark in specific rooms — said to a fellow CEO, said to suppliers in negotiations. QI ↗ documents a July 2013 tweet by Om Malik and an August 2014 Financial Times article carrying such framings, all of them after the 2012 Fortune piece, which itself names no occasion at all.
The line is sometimes spoken of as shareholder-letter gospel. It is not in his 2020 letter ↗, his last as chief executive, which reproduces the 1997 letter in full.

misattribution.truthLine: What is documented is this and only this: on 16 November 2012, Adam Lashinsky wrote in Fortune ↗ that “a favorite Bezos aphorism” is “Your margin is my opportunity.” Everything more specific than that — the date, the room, the listener — was added afterwards by other people.

context.heading: Why the line travels so well
lead: Amazon’s whole competitive posture was an argument against comfortable profit margins. Where rivals treated a healthy margin as proof of a good business, Amazon treated it as slack in someone else’s system — room to undercut, absorb, and take the customer. Six words compress that entire strategy into something you can say across a dinner table, which is precisely why it spread.

The awkward part is that the compression may not be Bezos’s. The line enters the record in a journalist’s summary of how Bezos thinks, and every later citation traces back through that summary rather than around it. It is a genuine description of his strategy; whether it is a genuine transcription of his sentence is a different question, and nobody has answered it.
context.detailsSummary: How a reported aphorism hardens into a quotation
detailsBody: The mechanism is ordinary and hard to see from inside. A reporter with real access writes that a subject is fond of saying something. Readers reasonably treat that as testimony. The line then gets quotation marks, then a speaker tag, then an occasion — each retelling adding a little specificity that the original never contained.

Quote Investigator captures that hardening in progress: a July 2013 tweet by Om Malik placing the remark “in conversation with another CEO,” a September 2013 listicle ranking it among the smartest things Bezos ever said, and an August 2014 Financial Times piece situating it in meetings with suppliers. None of those supply the missing thing — a documented moment when Bezos said it.

This is not a debunking. Nothing here suggests Bezos did not say it, and a man who built a company on the principle may well have phrased it exactly this way many times. The honest position is narrower than the internet’s: widely credited, strategically authentic, source unlocated.
context.pull: The line is almost certainly Bezos-shaped. That is not the same as Bezos-sourced.
